extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of comparative mythology, folklore, and Indian religion (educated general audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and implicit standards for writing or presenting Sanskrit epic and Vedic material to a Western/readership: how to select, tone, and interpret myths; comparative-method cautions; and how to use epics as cultural sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone down miraculous elements; present dramatic phases fully
rubrics_metrics.description: The miraculous element is somewhat toned down in the accounts of conflicts, and the more dramatic phases of the heroic stories are presented in as full detail as space permits, so as to afford our readers glimpses of ancient life in northern India at a time when Vedic religion still held sway.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When excerpting or retelling epic material for readers, reduce excessive supernatural ornamentation in conflict scenes while preserving and elaborating dramatic/human details that illuminate daily life, social relations, and character. Example: emphasise hero songs and human episodes in the Rámáyana and Mahábhárata rather than only their miraculous aspects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach texts sympathetically (adopt the author's viewpoint)
rubrics_metrics.description: To appreciate fully the sacred and romantic literature of India, we should follow the advice of Robert Louis Stevenson: 'To learn aright from any teacher... we must first of all... think ourselves into sympathy with his position.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret texts on their own terms rather than through immediate European prejudices; seek the 'ruling spirit behind the code of rules' so the reader can conform or dissent from an informed perspective. This is an explicit hermeneutic prescription for readers and writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat epics as non-historical but rich cultural sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Although neither of these great works can be regarded as historical narratives, they contain a mass of historical matter which throws much light on the habits and customs and beliefs of the early peoples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use epic narratives as evidence for social practices, institutions, and values while avoiding treating them as straightforward documentary history. Extract customs, social roles, and material culture cautiously as indirect historical testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use comparative analysis to identify shared mythic motifs
rubrics_metrics.description: The hammer god, dragon-slayer, artisan god and other motifs recur across Eurasia (Indra ~ Thor ~ Zeus-pater ~ Ptah ~ P'an Ku ~ Bel-Merodach, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draw parallels across traditions by matching functional motifs (e.g., thunderer, world-artisan, dragon/serpent adversary) and trace distribution and local transformations; use multiple cross-cultural examples to support comparative claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh archaeological evidence and belief systems differently
rubrics_metrics.description: Bronze is, of course, of less ethnic significance than beliefs, but it is difficult to believe... that an isolated and poorly armed people could have imposed its intellectual culture over a wide area without having received anything in return.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat material culture (archaeology) and ideological/cognitive systems (beliefs, myths) as distinct kinds of evidence. Avoid over-interpreting archaeological similarity as proof of direct ethnic or intellectual dominance; consider reciprocal influence and differing significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer common-source or cultural-diffusion explanations over simplistic racial imposition
rubrics_metrics.description: It is more probable that the northern Germanic peoples were subjected to the same influences which are traceable in their mythology and in the Vedic hymns, from a common source, and there may be more than mere mythology in the persistent tradition that the ancestors of the Teutons immigrated from Asia led by Odin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When similar mythic motifs appear in distant areas, consider shared sources or diffusion rather than assuming one culture imposed beliefs by racial migration. Treat traditions of migration cautiously and allow for cultural (not purely racial) movements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use geographic/racial distribution to assess independent origin vs diffusion
rubrics_metrics.description: The Upanishadic doctrine of metempsychosis is less likely to have been so much coincidental as racial when we find that it is restricted to those areas where definite racial influences must have been at work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a doctrine or motif arose independently or via diffusion by checking its geographic and cultural distribution; clustering in particular racial/ethnic areas strengthens arguments for transmission or shared racial influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about claiming direct lineage between similar myths
rubrics_metrics.description: The Indian Vedic and Epic dragon-slaying stories have evidently no connection, however, with a lost Creation myth. It is possible that they are part of the floating material from which Babylonian mythology was framed. Indra bears points of resemblance to Bel-Merodach, but he is not a Creator in the sublime sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge resemblance without overstating genealogical descent; allow for 'floating material' and complex reworking. Use specific functional and contextual differences (e.g., Indra is artisan/warrior, not Creator) to qualify comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highlight humanizing and ethical features to counteract Western preconceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The civilization revealed by the narrative poems was of no mean order... No such barbaric incident occurs in the Mahábhárata battles as when in the Iliad Achilles drags the body of Hector; Arjuna honours his fallen foe and performs rites at the funeral pyre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When presenting non-Western epics to a Western audience, foreground elements (chivalry, respect for the dead, familial devotion) that correct stereotypes of 'barbarism' and demonstrate moral/social complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use ritual and narrative detail to illustrate social practices
rubrics_metrics.description: At the barley harvest in spring and the rice harvest in autumn offerings were made to the gods... The fee of the priest was the first-born calf 'for that is, as it were, the firstfruits of the cattle'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include concrete ritual descriptions (offerings, priestly fees, harvest customs, competitive rites) from texts to reconstruct economic, religious, and social practices. These specifics make epics useful for cultural history.
